issues.issue: The Application is "incorporated herein by reference" as a warranted document, which sits awkwardly with provision 24.1's statement that this Contract is the entire agreement superseding all prior writings. A court could be asked whether the Application's contents form part of the agreement.

The defined "Contract Year" runs thirteen months in its first iteration, which has to be applied to provision 14.2's liquidated damages of "$750,000 per Contract Year, pro rated" and 14.5's dates. A court measuring damages would have to construe how the irregular first Contract Year meshes with those clauses.

"May consider an extension" in the University's "sole discretion" gives no ascertainable obligation beyond meeting, so the extension promise's content is uncertain. The duty to "discuss ... the desirability of a possible extension" cannot be measured.

Salary is payable "as compensation for his services ... and satisfactory performance of the terms and conditions of this Contract," which can be read either as recital of purpose or as a condition precedent to payment. "Satisfactory performance" is undefined and unmeasured.

The promise of "standard staff fringe benefits" per the Staff Handbook has to be squared with provision 24.2(d), under which the University reserves the right to modify benefits unilaterally. A court could be asked which controls.

"A mutually agreed upon golf or country club" supplies no fallback if the parties never agree, leaving the obligation's object undetermined. The scope of "development and entertainment activities associated with ... official responsibilities" is also unbounded.

"All Operating expenses ... including without limitation, gasoline and oil" pairs a general term with two consumable specifics, leaving unclear whether items like insurance, maintenance or repairs fall inside it. The University separately promises the car will be "fully insured" in 3.4, sharpening that boundary question.

The bonus structure is mechanically broken: "The greatest of" introduces (1)-(3) but items (2) and (3) are both $100,000, the "B" designation is missing before the conference-championship bonus, and the connectors alternate between "or" and "and." Whether the bonuses are alternative or cumulative cannot be read off the text.

The $150,000 is payable "while the Employee is representing the University as Head Football Coach" in semi-annual installments, which must be reconciled with provision 14.10's cessation of all payments on termination and with 14.2's liquidated-damages measure. Whether this sum forms part of the compensation base after an early termination is left open.

The paragraph sits in provision 3.9 but refers to "the matters described in, this provision 3.8," a mis-numbered cross-reference. The scope of the publicity-rights grant turns on which provision's subject matter it attaches to.

The duty to devote "full time, attention and energies" must be squared with provision 10.1, which permits the Employee to contract independently with outside sources and run football camps under 9.0. The clause's own "subject to any exceptions hereinafter expressly described" leaves the boundary to be construed.

Item (9), "such other duties as assigned from time to time by the University's Director of Athletics," is an open catch-all appended to eight specific duties, and its reach against those specifics is undefined. Duties (7) and (8) — "good working relationship" and public relations that "reflect positively" — are themselves unmeasurable standards.

"If the Employee is found to be in ... violation of NCAA Rules" does not say who makes the finding or by what process, and "significant or repetitive violations" is an unmeasured threshold for termination. Both terms would have to be construed before the discipline power could be applied.

"Competing shows or programs" is undefined, and against the extremely broad definition of "Programs" in 8.2 (any medium whose subject is in whole or in part the Team or University athletics) its boundary is genuinely uncertain. Whether a general media appearance is "competing" could be read either way.

The $350,000 is payable "while the Employee is representing the University as Head Football Coach" but is also stated as an annual amount "during each Contract Year," which must be reconciled with 14.2's $750,000 liquidated-damages figure and 14.10's cessation of payments. Whether it counts toward post-termination compensation is left unresolved.

The sentence breaks off mid-clause ("the University shall have the right (and shall"), so the scope of the consent granted is textually incomplete. It also cross-refers only to provisions 8.1 and 8.2, omitting 8.3, although the preceding paragraph covered 8.1-8.3.

The provision begins mid-sentence ("form acceptable to the University; naming the University as an additional insured") with no subject or operative verb, so the conditions it imposes and on whom cannot be identified from the text. The insurance and indemnity obligations it recites are unattached to any duty-holder.

The paragraph first prohibits all public use of the Employee's publicity rights without approval, then says "Without limiting the foregoing, the Employee shall be permitted to contract independently with outside sources," a permission that on its face qualifies the prohibition it purports not to limit. Whether outside endorsement contracts are permitted or barred turns on that internal contradiction.

The statement that changes in NCAA, conference or University rules "shall automatically apply to this Contract without the necessity of a written modification" cannot be squared with provision 24.1, which bars amendment or modification except by a writing signed by both parties. A court would have to decide which governs a rule change that alters the Employee's obligations.

The caption "Employee Retains all Revenues" is contradicted by the body, which subjects retention to limitations in this Contract and in University, conference and NCAA rules, and the reporting list ("including, but not limited to, income from annuities, sports camps ...") leaves the catch-all's reach unclear. Provision 21.1 says captions do not control, but the tension still requires construction.

"Usurp any corporate opportunities of the University" and "any activity causing a conflict of interest" are undefined and have no evident content for a university athletics employee. Both boundaries would have to be construed before the prohibition could be applied.

The bar on carrying or being paid for unused vacation must be reconciled with provision 3.2's grant of "standard staff fringe benefits" under the Staff Handbook, which may treat accrued vacation differently. Provision 11.1's own exclusivity paragraph is the intended answer, but the interaction still invites argument.

The exclusivity sentence overrides "anything contained herein" on vacation, which must be read against provision 3.2's incorporation of Staff Handbook fringe benefits. The "notwithstanding" language most likely resolves it, but the overlap is the sort a court is asked to reconcile.

The clause guarantees an "allotted budget" of "not less than One Million Nine Hundred Thousand Dollars" and in the same breath requires the Employee to keep staff costs "within the University's allotted budget," without saying whether the allotted budget is the $1.9 million floor or some other figure the University sets. The same phrase does two inconsistent jobs.

"Just cause" is the operative trigger for termination without any payment, and the clause lets the University terminate "at any time" on that ground; whether particular conduct meets it is the classic construction question. The provision itself supplies no standard, deferring to the definition that follows and to the term's "normally understood meaning."

The promise that the University is "relieved of all further obligations (financial and otherwise)" must be read against provision 14.10, which preserves obligations "expressly described in provisions 14.2, 14.3, 14.4, 14.7, and 14.8," and against the survival clauses. What survives a just-cause termination is not stated consistently.

Subsection F makes "just cause" include, "as determined by the University," conduct "seriously prejudicial to the best interests of the University," conduct that "brings the University into disrepute," or that reflects "moral turpitude" — each an unmeasured standard, and the self-judging phrase makes it unclear whether the University's determination is conclusive or reviewable. This is the language on which a wrongful-termination dispute would turn.

Subsection A limits criminal conduct to "any conduct by Employee resulting in his conviction of a violation of a criminal statute," yet the opening words add "its normally understood meaning in employment contracts" and F sweeps in any disreputable conduct. Whether the specific conviction requirement of A confines the general catch-alls (expressio unius) is squarely open.

Liquidated damages are fixed "in, and only in, the amount of Seven Hundred Fifty Thousand Dollars ($750,000) per Contract Year, pro rated, for the then-unexpired Term," a figure that neither matches the base salary nor the total contractual compensation, and "pro rated" is not tied to any stated period. The measure of recovery on a no-cause termination therefore requires construction.

The exclusive "in, and only in" damages measure sits against provision 24.6, under which all remedies are cumulative and none limits any other. A court would have to decide whether 14.2 caps the Employee's recovery.

The mitigation offset — obligations "shall cease" once the Employee begins other employment, with only a shortfall payable — cannot be squared on its face with provision 14.2's promise of liquidated damages "in, and only in" a fixed amount that "shall survive" termination. The "notwithstanding" opener signals the drafters knew the two pull apart.

The trigger is that the Employee "unilaterally resign or otherwise terminate his employment," a phrase whose boundary against a University-initiated departure or constructive discharge is not drawn. The parenthetical thirty-day notice duty is embedded in the trigger without saying what follows if notice is not given.

This clause terminates "the University's obligations, financial and otherwise" immediately on disability, yet provision 14.10 lists 14.8 among the provisions whose payment obligations expressly survive termination. The two cannot both be given their literal effect.

The list of surviving payment obligations — "provisions 14.2, 14.3, 14.4, 14.7, and 14.8" — includes 14.4 and 14.8, which by their own terms cut off or terminate payments rather than create them, and omits other operative provisions. The exception list cannot be reconciled with the clauses it names.

The restraint covers football employment "within the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania and/or at any other Big East Conference ... member-institution," and the "and/or" leaves the geographic reach genuinely uncertain. It is also triggered only by resignation, so its application to other modes of departure is unclear.

The Contract is said to be "governed by" unidentified "principles and precepts and regulations that relate to equal Opportunity employment," with no source named. Whether this creates contractual obligations enforceable beyond statute cannot be determined from the words.

"Private information" is defined as anything "known by Employee as a consequence of his employment, and not generally known outside the University," a definition with no subject-matter limit at all. Its outer boundary would have to be construed before any disclosure duty could be enforced.

The perpetual bar on using or disclosing private information has no legal-compulsion carve-out, because provision 17.3's exception is expressed to apply only "notwithstanding anything contained in provision 17.1." Whether 17.3 also relieves the 17.2 duty is left open.

The required-disclosure exception is expressed only against "provision 17.1," leaving the broader private-information covenant in provision 17.2 without any carve-out for disclosure compelled by law. Naming one confidentiality provision and not the other invites an expressio unius argument about 17.2.

Notice is to be given to "the Director of Athletics at his/her University address" and to the Employee at "his University address," without any street address, so the place of effective notice is not fixed by the writing. Whether notice sent elsewhere is effective would have to be construed.

The declaration that the Executive Vice Chancellor's decision is "final" and that this is the "exclusive" grievance mechanism has to be read with the immediately following paragraph preserving each party's right to go to court in Allegheny County. The word "internally" is the intended reconciliation, but the finality language pulls the other way.

The permissive "nothing herein shall prevent" is coupled with a consent that "jurisdiction and venue for any such action shall be in" Allegheny County, so it is unclear whether the forum provision is permissive or mandatory. That must also be read against 20.1's "exclusive" internal grievance procedure.

The requirement that "all disputes and grievances shall be treated confidentially by both parties, at all times" cannot be fully squared with the immediately preceding paragraph permitting either party to submit disputes to a public federal or state court. A court would have to decide what confidentiality survives litigation.

The no-modification sentence reads "shall not be released , discharged, amended or modified ; many manner," a garbled rendering of "in any manner" that leaves the sentence ungrammatical. The scope of the writing requirement depends on repairing that text.

The requirement that the Contract be amended only "by an instrument in writing signed by both of the parties" conflicts with provision 10.1B, under which changes in NCAA, conference or University rules "shall automatically apply to this Contract without the necessity of a written modification." The two cannot both be applied literally.

Subparagraph (d) reserves to the University a unilateral "right to modify benefits hereunder," which cannot be squared with provision 24.1's bar on modification except by a writing signed by both parties, nor with 3.2's benefits promise. Which prevails would have to be decided.

The excuse covers "events beyond its reasonable control" illustrated by an open list ("may include, but shall not be limited to, acts of God, war, civil commotion, fire, flood or other casualty and government regulation or restriction"), so the catch-all's reach against the enumerated specifics is uncertain. The closing proviso then requires performance to be "impossible or unreasonably difficult," a different and stricter test than the opening "unable to perform."

The declaration that all remedies are cumulative and "none of them shall be in limitation of any other" pulls against provision 14.2, which fixes the Employee's entitlement "in, and only in" a stated liquidated sum, and against 14.5's lump-sum liquidated damages. Whether the liquidated-damages clauses are exclusive is left in doubt.
